extracted.intended_audience: operators and creators of algorithms (computer programmers, industry leaders), policymakers, regulators, and civil society organizations
extracted.subtask_description: A policy and best-practices framework for identifying, detecting, and mitigating algorithmic bias in machine learning systems, plus public-policy recommendations (laws, sandboxes, safe harbors) to reduce consumer harms. Targets the design, testing, governance, and oversight activities of algorithm operators and regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic hygiene (framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A framework which identifies specific causes of biases and employs best practices to identify and mitigate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algorithmic hygiene as an organizing concept: surface and address bias up front to avert harms and liabilities. The paper draws on roundtable input to juxtapose developer concerns and policymaker interests and offers self-regulatory practices, public policy recommendations, and consumer-focused strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias — working definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias: outcomes which are systematically less favorable to individuals within a particular group and where there is no relevant difference between groups that justifies such harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat bias broadly to include disparate treatment and disparate impact; use this as the baseline to decide when mitigation is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical human biases as a cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical human biases shaped by pervasive prejudices can be reproduced and amplified in computer models (e.g., policing disparities reflected in COMPAS; male-dominated hiring benchmarks reflected in Amazon’s recruiting tool).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that past discriminatory patterns in human institutions will be reflected in training data and can perpetuate or amplify harms unless explicitly corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete or unrepresentative training data
rubrics_metrics.description: Insufficient or unrepresentative training data causes algorithmic predictions to be systematically worse for under-represented groups (e.g., poor recognition of darker-skinned faces due to under-representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess training data diversity and reliability; collect additional representative data where needed; consider data lifecycle and sampling biases; test across diverse populations and settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-representation and skewed datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-representation of a group in datasets can skew decisions and increase false matches for that group (e.g., African-Americans over-represented in mug-shot databases leading to more false matches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze dataset composition for both under- and over-representation and the distinct harms each can cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of sensitive information
rubrics_metrics.description: All detection approaches should begin with careful handling of users' sensitive information, including membership in federally protected groups and other groups susceptible to harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance privacy/regulatory constraints (e.g., GDPR) with the need to use sensitive attributes for detection; consider regulatory sandboxes or safe harbors to permit testing when privacy rules would otherwise prohibit beneficial uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting bias via outcome comparisons and simulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine algorithm outputs to check for anomalous results; compare outcomes for different groups and run simulations (including simulated true and false predictions) before deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider secondary data collection and simulation because models may behave differently in the wild; use simulations to detect disparities and anomalous behavior before real-world application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of error rates and selection of fairness metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare equality of error rates across groups (but recognize that not all error rates can be equalized simultaneously), and choose which error rates to prioritize based on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish principled rules for which error rates should be equalized in particular situations; document trade-offs and rationale because different stakeholders may focus on different metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs between fairness and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are inherent tensions between minimizing harm (fairness) and optimizing accuracy or public-safety objectives; optimizing for one can adversely affect the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ways to reduce disparities without sacrificing overall performance where possible; analyze social costs of trade-offs; involve human decision-makers when algorithmic trade-offs are ethically or socially sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms and proxies for sensitive attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms may use proxies (e.g., zip code) that stand in for sensitive attributes and produce discriminatory outcomes even if the algorithm is not given the sensitive attribute explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit models for proxy variables, be transparent about potential proxies, and evaluate whether proxies create legal or ethical classification harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in handling sensitive information
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must be more transparent in their handling of sensitive attributes and potential proxies, especially where proxies could be a legal classificatory harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose data practices and rationale for using or not using sensitive attributes; enable external scrutiny where feasible (audits, explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensitive attributes for detection/mitigation (with guardrails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using sensitive attributes in modeling can be a strategy for detecting and curing biases, but doing so may be constrained by privacy rules—hence propose regulatory sandboxes and safe harbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where legal and privacy constraints allow, permit controlled use of sensitive attributes (e.g., in sandboxes) to identify disparate outcomes; provide legal safe harbors to enable this diagnostic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical governance principles (trustworthy AI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt governance principles such as the EU’s seven: (1) human agency and oversight, (2) technical robustness and safety, (3) privacy and data governance, (4) transparency, (5) diversity, nondiscrimination and fairness, (6) environmental and societal well-being, (7) accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these high-level ethical principles as guardrails for system lifecycle design and policy; accept that fairness is a human and ethical determination requiring human involvement for consequential decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update nondiscrimination and civil-rights laws for the digital space
rubrics_metrics.description: Nondiscrimination laws should be updated to interpret and redress online disparate impacts and clarify how existing statutory protections apply to algorithmic decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative clarity helps operators design systems that avoid triggering legally recognizable harms and aligns technical design with non-negotiable legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory sandboxes and safe harbors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use regulatory sandboxes to foster anti-bias experimentation and create safe harbors to allow use of sensitive information when detecting and mitigating biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sandboxes permit testing under controlled regulatory flexibility; safe harbors reduce legal risk for operators trying to detect/mitigate bias using otherwise restricted data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a bias impact statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators should develop a bias impact statement as a self-regulatory practice to probe and avert potential biases across design, implementation, and monitoring phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bias impact statement should document initial assumptions, purpose, process, production, which automated decisions require scrutiny, operator incentives, stakeholder engagement, and be developed by cross-functional teams. It can be used to filter decisions that need extra vetting prior to development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which automated decisions require scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by asking whether an automated decision could have negative or unintended outcomes, for whom, and the severity of consequences; consult legal protections (housing, employment, credit, criminal justice, health) as filters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize scrutiny for decisions with potential legal, social, or economic harms; constantly question legal liabilities and societal effects when deciding to automate or modify automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias impact statement — template design questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Design-phase questions for the bias impact statement include: What will the automated decision do? Who is the audience and who will be most affected? Do we have training data to make correct predictions? Is the training data sufficiently diverse and reliable? What is the data lifecycle of the algorithm? Which groups are we worried about when it comes to training?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the template questions to systematically surface potential harms and data issues; apply flexibly across phases and document answers for accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic impact assessments (AIAs) and multi-stage review
rubrics_metrics.description: AIAs: multi-round review processes (internal, external, public) that identify potential harms, require notice to impacted populations and a comment period if bias occurs, and support users' right to challenge algorithmic decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AIA processes to create substantive feedback loops; combine AIA with bias impact statements to provide forethought and oversight across lifecycle stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement and advisory councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage users early and throughout development, include civil society organizations, and consider advisory councils to add ground-level perspective and predict biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder engagement improves selection of inputs/outputs and helps anticipate harms; civil-society engagement can prevent escalation to press/regulators and provides legitimacy to design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-functional and interdisciplinary teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish cross-functional teams (technical, legal, policy, civil-society expertise) to create and implement bias impact statements and oversee design and monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diverse teams can better identify risk vectors, improve design choices, and interpret fairness trade-offs; include external technical experts where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive design principles and diversity in teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt inclusive design principles and increase diversity among programmers and data scientists to reduce under-representation and blind spots in training sample selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity in teams helps detect potential exclusions and produces richer training samples; inclusive design aims to avoid excluding inputs and to include affected voices in design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous testing across settings and products
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject algorithms to rigorous testing (including testing multiple products/configurations/settings) to reveal errors and biases (example: Buolamwini’s facial-analysis testing across products and settings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for product error rates stratified by group, replicate experiments in varied contexts, and correct bugs that may improve both fairness and accuracy when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation and secondary data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulate predictions and consider a secondary data collection process because models may emit different behaviors when deployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulations can detect unequal average scores or other anomalies that warrant further investigation before live deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and recognition for good algorithmic hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators with practices that generate fairer outcomes should be recognized by policymakers and consumers and potentially rewarded for effective algorithmic hygiene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create incentives (public acknowledgment, certification) to motivate companies to invest in bias detection/mitigation and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic literacy and consumer-focused feedback mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote algorithmic literacy among users and create formal feedback mechanisms to allow civil society and users to report harms or challenge decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educate users about algorithmic behavior and provide accessible channels for complaints and remediation; tie feedback loops into AIA and bias impact statements.
